summary: Secure firmware updates are needed to fix vulnerabilities in Internet of Things devices, including constrained ones. This informational document describes the information that must be in a manifest, a concise machine-processable metadata document that describes the firmware image or images and protects them.

eli5.summary: Before a gadget installs an update, it needs a label saying what the update is and that it is real. This document lists what that label should say.

subtitle: What information a device needs to securely install a firmware update.

tldr.problem: Internet of Things devices must receive secure firmware updates over the network to fix vulnerabilities, but constrained devices have limited memory and processing power. A device needs to know what it is installing, verify it is legitimate, and ensure it does not get tricked into installing old or malicious firmware.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a manifest: a concise, machine-readable metadata document that travels with a firmware image, signed to prove authenticity. The manifest lists what information must be present—vendor and device identifiers, sequence numbers, payload digests, storage location, security keys, and more—to protect against threats like rollback attacks, signature spoofing, and installation to the wrong location.
tldr.outcome: The RFC provides a blueprint for firmware update systems. It does not define the encoding (CBOR, JSON, etc.) but specifies what fields must exist and why, driven by security requirements and user stories covering diverse IoT scenarios.

today: RFC 9124 is an Informational document describing a manifest information model for firmware updates. It is informational guidance for implementors and is not a protocol standard itself. Various IoT firmware update systems reference this model.

sections.title: Firmware Updates for Constrained Devices
sections.content:
IoT devices must remain secure throughout their lifetime. They need firmware updates to fix vulnerabilities, change configuration, and add features. Unlike traditional servers that can store large executables, many IoT devices are constrained: they have limited memory (kilobytes), processing power, and battery life. A firmware manifest is a concise, machine-readable metadata document bundled with the firmware image. It describes what the firmware is, protects it cryptographically, and enables secure installation.

This RFC describes an information model—what fields the manifest must contain and why—without specifying how they are encoded (CBOR, JSON, XML, etc.). Each field is motivated by threats and user stories, ensuring the manifest is both secure and practical for constrained devices. Not all fields apply to all scenarios; implementations choose which are necessary.
sections.eli5: IoT devices are tiny computers with little memory. They need a secure way to get updates. The manifest is a label that says what the update is and proves it is real so the device can safely install it.

sections.title: The Manifest: Information Elements and Envelope
sections.content:
A manifest consists of required and optional information elements: fields that carry data about the firmware and its installation. Key elements include:

  • Version ID: Which version of the manifest format (REQUIRED)
  • Monotonic Sequence Number: Prevents rollback—an attacker cannot trick a device into installing old firmware (REQUIRED)
  • Vendor ID and Class ID: Identify the vendor and device type to prevent firmware intended for one product from being installed on another (RECOMMENDED)
  • Payload Format: Describes the firmware format—raw binary, compressed, encrypted, etc. (REQUIRED)
  • Payload Digest: A hash of the firmware allowing the device to verify it was not corrupted (REQUIRED)
  • Storage Location: Where the device should write the firmware (REQUIRED)
  • Signature: Cryptographic proof the manifest came from a trusted authority (REQUIRED)
  • Processing Steps: Instructions for decompression, decryption, etc. (RECOMMENDED)

Additional elements support features like metadata about the update, text descriptions for users, dependency chains for multi-party authorization, and encryption keys. The manifest itself may be protected in an Envelope that bundles the manifest with its signature and delegation chain.
sections.eli5: The manifest lists facts about the firmware: who made it, what device it is for, how big it is, a checksum, and a digital signature proving it is real.

sections.title: Security and Usability Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC derives manifest fields from a comprehensive threat model using STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege). Examples of threats and their mitigations:

  • Rollback attack: An attacker sends old firmware with a known vulnerability. Mitigation: Monotonic sequence numbers ensure only newer firmware is accepted.
  • Mismatched firmware: Wrong firmware for the device type. Mitigation: Vendor ID and Class ID must match.
  • Installation to wrong location: Firmware written to wrong memory area breaks the device. Mitigation: Storage Location field authenticated in the signature.
  • Malicious firmware: Untrusted firmware changes the device's Class ID to allow future malicious updates. Mitigation: Signature proof only authorized parties can modify critical fields.

Usability requirements include pre-installation checks (can the device apply this update?), version matching (install only on the right firmware version), component updates (some devices have multiple updatable parts), and delegated authority (allow representatives to sign on behalf of the vendor). The manifest supports all these scenarios while remaining small enough for constrained devices.
sections.eli5: The manifest prevents lots of attacks: old firmware getting installed, firmware for the wrong device, firmware being stored in the wrong place, and fake firmware from untrusted sources.

sections.title: Advanced Manifest Features
sections.content:
The RFC covers several advanced capabilities:

  • Encryption: For sensitive firmware (e.g., proprietary algorithms), the payload can be encrypted. The manifest includes or references the decryption key.
  • Multiple components: Devices may have an OS, bootloader, and application, each updateable separately. Dependencies specify which components must be present for an update to apply.
  • Metadata: Rich information returned during name resolution includes caching policy, security parameters, data format, and alternative locations.
  • Expiration: Firmware can expire after a date, preventing devices from installing obsolete updates.
  • Delegation: A chain of authorization tokens allows delegation of signing authority, so manufacturers can delegate to regional distributors or customers can delegate to management systems.

These features make the manifest flexible for diverse IoT scenarios: simple single-component devices, complex systems with multiple parties, offline devices, mobile producers, and different trust models.
sections.eli5: Advanced features include hiding the firmware code with encryption, updating different parts of the device separately, setting expiration dates, and allowing trusted partners to sign updates.

sections.title: Implementing the Manifest Information Model
sections.content:
Implementors need not include all fields. The RFC defines which elements are REQUIRED (must be present in any manifest format), RECOMMENDED (should be supported unless there is a specific reason not to), and OPTIONAL (selected based on the threat model and user stories for a given scenario).

For example, a simple device in a controlled environment might need only: version ID, sequence number, vendor ID, class ID, payload format, payload digest, size, storage location, and signature. A complex system might add expiration, processing steps, dependencies, delegation chains, and encryption.

The information model is independent of encoding. Different serializations (CBOR, JSON, protobuf, etc.) can implement these elements. The key benefit is that all implementations cover the same security and usability ground, avoiding gaps where one encoding omits important fields.
sections.eli5: Different devices need different fields. A simple device might only need the basics, while a complex system needs more features. The manifest can be encoded many ways as long as it includes the right information.
